BOI.excerpt: A compact shortwave upper trough will approach the Pacific NW on Monday and bring a return closer to normal temperatures, along with another round of precipitation to the region Monday evening into Tuesday.

sections.name: Key Messages
paragraphs: - Cool and dry this weekend, frost and freeze possible Saturday and Sunday mornings in lower valleys.
- Seasonable temperatures with an unsettled pattern bringing a chance of rain and high mountain snow early next week.

sections.name: Short Term
paragraphs: Drier conditions will set up over the weekend under a west- southwest flow. Clearing skies and lighter winds tonight will support near freezing temperatures in lower Snake Plain Saturday morning. Sheltered locations are more likely to see frost with cold spots touching freezing. This will be the case again on Sunday morning as well, though a moderating air mass and the introduction of high clouds could limit coverage. Saturday is cool and breezy, but not as windy as today. Southwest flow sets up on Sunday as a low pressure system approaches the Pac NW coast. This shift will bring warmer temperatures and increase easterly winds across open terrain. Moisture in the southwest flow aloft will increase high cloud cover, starting across SE Oregon late Saturday. Temperatures are near normal Saturday (~60 in valleys and ~50 in mtn valleys) warming to around 5 degrees above normal on Sunday.

sections.name: Long Term
paragraphs: A compact shortwave upper trough will approach the Pacific NW on Monday and bring a return closer to normal temperatures, along with another round of precipitation to the region Monday evening into Tuesday. There are still some timing differences amongst deterministic model guidance - most notably the ECMWF which is faster and depicts a secondary upstream system off the BC coast - but probabilistic guidance favors Tuesday as the more active day, especially into west-central and central Idaho. QPF amounts are generally expected to remain near or below 0.25 inch even in the mountains, given the lack of a significant moisture tap. Snow levels will remain above 6000 feet throughout this event as well, which will limit snow accumulations primarily to higher elevation mountainous areas. Temperatures will modulate during the week and remain slightly above seasonal normals. In the wake of the early week system, the pattern will remain unsettled, with low-end (up to 20%) probabilities maintained each day, especially in the mountains. The next significant storm system takes shape Thursday and Friday. Moisture will remain quite limited and remain confined to the Desert Southwest, with precipitation chances beginning to increase again on Friday.

CYS.name: Cheyenne
CYS.excerpt: Active weather will characterize the first few days of the long term period from Monday through Tuesday night. On Monday morning, weak surface troughing will extend from the New Mexico high plains northward through Colorado and western Nebraska.

sections.name: Key Messages
paragraphs: - A High Wind Warning in effect until 3 PM for Carbon County and a very small portion of Albany County.
- Above average highs this afternoon, but a cold front will drop temperatures to around 5 to 10 degrees below normal for the weekend.
- Near normal temperatures and a bit warmer by Tuesday into Wednesday, but next Pacific system will be approaching from the Pacific Northwest by the middle of the week.

sections.name: Short Term
paragraphs: This weekend split flow will continue to decline our precipitation chances as moisture gets pushed just to our east. The pattern through the forecast period will consist of the split in flow as upper level troughing lifts up and combines with Canadian troughing, with a very quick transient ridge building over the area on Saturday, but the other half of the split flow in the form of a cutoff low will be moving into the Four Corners, becoming the focal point for our forecast through Monday evening. At the surface, a cold front moves across this evening and should fully pass through our region by Saturday morning, with some high pressure overtaking in its wake but multiple shortwaves passing across through the weekend.

Under this pattern, we'll see a quick chance of precipitation this evening along the trough axis and a weak boundary setting up across the Nebraska Panhandle and draping down through Laramie County. Have included some shower chances across this area, but expected those to be isolated to possibly scattered with minimal QPF accumulations. This flow is also struggling to show meaningful precipitation in the high terrain as the jet weakens this afternoon and evening and flow begins to lower in response, and CAMs are not indicating we'll see anything meaningful in this region alongside NBM guidance. The next noteworthy batch of precipitation is expected Saturday evening into Sunday under southerly to southwesterly flow as moisture begins to return, and continues through Sunday night into Monday. The issue will be the fact that the bulk of this moisture gets pushed to our east, and without a strong forcing mechanism over the area we'll struggle to get much more than scattered weak showers through this period. Latest QPF analysis shows only widespread precipitation totals in the 0.1-0.2 inch range, with Cheyenne County expected to be the "big winner" as this area will be closest to the better moisture in Central Nebraska with totals nearing 0.3-0.5 inch. Accounting for bias correction, this could even be on the high side, but taking a look at ensembles, it appears that most guidance errs on the side of 0.1-0.4 inch widespread which would at least give the hope for some much needed moisture, but don't bank on a soaker. The bulk of this also falls either in the high terrain or east, so lower elevations in Carbon and Albany Counties may be sitting this one out.

Outside of precipitation, our cold front will bring notably cooler temperatures as highs sit around 5 to 10 degrees below normal on both Saturday and Sunday, with widespread highs in the 50's to 40's and overnight lows in the 30's. These near freezing to freezing conditions could even encourage some wintry precipitation to mix in with morning rain, but a few flurries and rain/snow mix are the most that is expected out of this currently. Finally, the gusty conditions we've seen today should persist through Saturday morning as the pressure gradients shift eastwards, but by the afternoon winds should be relaxing with relatively benign speeds for this region to conclude the weekend.

sections.name: Long Term
paragraphs: Active weather will characterize the first few days of the long term period from Monday through Tuesday night. On Monday morning, weak surface troughing will extend from the New Mexico high plains northward through Colorado and western Nebraska. Seasonably high surface moisture will be in place with ensemble guidance supporting PWAT values on the order of 1-2 sigma. The center of a ridge of high pressure will be located in the northern high plains, resulting in broad easterly flow around its base including western Nebraska and eastern Wyoming. These factors combined will result in overcast conditions with numerous clouds and showers around throughout the day. Ensemble guidance is mixed as to liquid totals given a lack of a well- defined surface low over the high plains. This is currently resulting in a highly dispersive forecast with some guidance supporting a moderate to heavy rainfall event east of I-25 through the NE panhandle and another large group of ensemble members keeping this event less organized and farther east. Some forecast guidance members, particularly the operational ECMWF, indicate a potential overlap between cold temperatures in east- northeasterly flow and heavier QPF, enough to produce some light snowfall on the order of 1-3 inches for east-central Wyoming and the northern Nebraska panhandle. Currently, this outcome appears to be somewhat of an outlier compared to the rest of guidance. Overall, with weak forcing aloft and a lack of a more defined surface feature, we will favor the drier (and less snowy) end of the guidance package for the Monday timeframe. Still, abundant cloud cover and east-northeasterly flow should keep temperatures around 10 to 15 degrees cooler than average for Monday. This messy, disorganized system drifts east of the region on Monday night, with any lingering shower activity ending possibly as early as 6 to 9pm. After a partly cloudy overnight, attention quickly turns to our next system moving from the Great Basin into southwest Wyoming on Tuesday afternoon. Unlike the Monday event, this system will feature a potent mid/upper level low pressure center and faster wind speeds aloft. However, recent ensemble guidance trends continue to show very little precipitation making it to the ground outside of the mountains with this system as it translates eastward on Tuesday evening and overnight. In the Snowy, Sierra Madre, and northern Laramie ranges, current model QPF averages are around 0.1 to 0.2 inches of liquid. As this system exits eastward on Tuesday night, a fast jet stream in the 700-500mb layer is indicated by most guidance in an west-east orientation across southeast Wyoming. Given the favorable flow orientation, upper-level pattern and wind speeds aloft it is possible that a higher-wind event may be in the works for the Wednesday timeframe over the wind prone locations of southeast Wyoming. Dry zonal to north-westerly flow will resume over the region from Thursday through the end of the week with limited impacts expected.

GJT.name: Grand Junction
GJT.excerpt: As we move towards next week, models are also in fairly good agreement that dry zonal flow will begin to propagate through the region by Monday.

sections.name: Key Messages
paragraphs: - Flooding is ongoing across portions of southeast Utah and southwest Colorado, and is expected to continue through Saturday.
- While some rivers have crested, some rivers will experience their crest Saturday.
- Isolated to scattered showers and storms are expected Saturday. They will be capable of producing moderate to heavy rainfall that could result in additional flooding.
- A few storms may be capable of producing strong winds and large hail Saturday afternoon.

sections.name: Discussion
paragraphs: ONGOING FLOODING WITH MORE RAINFALL THIS WEEKEND:

The low pressure system responsible for pulling in the tropical moisture that resulted in the abundant rainfall the last couple days is sitting over southern California and Nevada. This low pressure system is expected to move into Arizona by Saturday afternoon and lift northeast across Utah and western Colorado during the day on Sunday and exiting to the northeast by Monday morning. As this happens, the low pressure system will pull another round of moisture around the low from the southeast on Saturday. The latest hi-res CAMs indicate convection developing across southeast Utah and southwest Colorado overnight into Saturday morning with more scattered to widespread showers and storms spreading further north Saturday afternoon and evening, favoring areas along and south of I-70. While the deep tropical moisture has vacated the region, PWAT anomalies with this push of moisture are projected to be around 200 percent of normal, which while not as high as a few days ago, is still enough to cause issues and heavy rainfall. The main concern is that many areas are already saturated from previous rainfall and there is ongoing flooding with many rivers and creeks running high. So any additional rainfall, especially where stronger convection occurs could result in more flooding and continuation of ongoing flooding. The rainfall amounts through Sunday are expected to range from 0.5-1.0 inches along the highway 160 corridor with slightly higher amounts in the mountains and lower amounts outside of southwest Colorado. While we could see gusty winds and hail with a few storms, the main concern is heavy rainfall. Hi res CAMs appear to show convection winding down Saturday night with some isolated showers lingering. Showers become more isolated to scattered on Sunday as the low pressure lifts overhead, but these showers are expected to be lighter than previous few days. Conditions begin to dry out Monday as this low lifts northeast over the Plains.

As we move towards next week, models are also in fairly good agreement that dry zonal flow will begin to propagate through the region by Monday. Because of this, we will be seeing cooler than normal temperatures, with the potential for overnight lows to drop below freezing for a couple hours at a time. Meanwhile, a low pressure system looks to enter the Pacific Northwest with a few shortwaves moving across the Northern Rockies through the week potentially bringing light showers to the north but overall, conditions appear to dry out until late next week when showers potentially return as a shortwave trough moves through the Desert SW and 4 Corners region pulling in some Pacific moisture. Keep in mind, this is still relatively far out, so confidence remains low on this matter as model solutions are varied.

PUB.name: Pueblo
PUB.excerpt: Tuesday through Friday...Broad southwest flow across the region will settle in for the remainder of the week.

sections.name: Key Messages
paragraphs: - Focus for heavier rainfall shifts to the eastern plains today and Sunday.
- Some accumulation snow possible across the higher peaks this afternoon through Sunday morning.
- Cooler and wetter weather areawide this weekend, with gradual warming and drying for the upcoming week.

sections.name: Short Term
paragraphs: Currently...Upper low is centered over southern CA late tonight, producing deep south-southwest flow across the region and drawing a healthy moisture plume up across New Mexico into southern CO. Showers and isolated thunderstorms are continuing across the southern mts and SE corner of the state through the overnight hours. Decided to drop the Flood Watch across the sw mts overnight since flood warnings are ongoing, but flood waters are gradually decreasing and additional warnings are not anticipated at this time. Temps are forecast to drop into the 30s for the high valleys and upper 40s to mid 50s for the plains by daybreak.

Today and tonight...Upper low will push into AZ through the day today, continuing the S-SW feed of moisture up into southern CO. Meanwhile, a cold front is forecast to drop south across the eastern plains through the morning, bringing much colder air to the forecast area with as much as a 20 degree drop in high temps across the plains. The upper low will gradually shift north to the northern AZ border through the evening. This positioning will be prime for continued precipitation across the forecast area through the day and night, though the heaviest rainfall amounts are expected to be across the far eastern plains. Though rain is still forecast along the Continental Divide today, especially in the afternoon, QPF amounts are coming in around half an inch over 24 hrs which should not force any additional flooding threats. Also, snow levels are dropping with new snow amounts of 5 to 8 inches possible across the mt peaks through the evening, so new snow means less of a runoff threat. Further east, heavier qpf amounts are expected, though totals have come down quite a bit from previous thinking. Latest totals are now ranging from 1 to almost 2 inches of additional rain through the day, which lessens the flooding threat and becomes more of a beneficial rain. WPC has painted much of the forecast area within a Slight area for excessive rainfall, and SPC has included portions of the eastern plains within a Marginal for severe storms, and the rest of the area in General Thunder. Plenty of shear available, but CAPE values are somewhat lacking, but the combination of a surface front and stronger S-SW flow aloft could make it sporty for a bit across the eastern plains. Main storm threats today will be gusty winds to 60 mph, hail nearing 1 inch in diameter, and periods of moderate to heavy rainfall.

Look for highs today in the mid 40s to around 50F for the high valleys, and 50s to lower 60s for the plains. Overnight minimum temps tonight will drop into the 30s for the high valleys, and 30s to lower 40s for the plains.

sections.name: Long Term
paragraphs: Sunday...Upper low pushes up into east central UT through the day Sunday, then weakens slightly and slides east into CO through the evening. Widespread showers and thunderstorms will continue across the forecast area through the afternoon, but the steering flow shifts from a S-SW direction to a more W-SW direction through late afternoon, keeping much of the stronger activity and highest QPF amounts right along the eastern border. The mt peaks may see an additional 1-2 inches of new snow, though snowfall is expected to really drop off. This should be the coolest day of the forecast period, with highs in the 50s for most locations, and nearing 60F for the far eastern plains.

Monday...Upper low weakens, opens and exits to the northeast through the day, with just some lingering isolated to low end scattered showers across the far eastern plains through the morning. Temps start to warm back up to near seasonal levels, with highs in the 50s to near 60F for the high valleys, and 60s for the plains.

Tuesday through Friday...Broad southwest flow across the region will settle in for the remainder of the week. A disturbance brushes by to the north on Tuesday, producing some brisk winds, otherwise conditions remain dry and temps remain seasonal as the Pacific moisture tap is temporarily shut down and moisture from the Gulf starts creeping northward towards the TX and OK panhandles. Moore

SLC.name: Salt Lake City
SLC.excerpt: Weak ridging is then expected to move over Utah during the day on Monday, bringing dry conditions with maxes near seasonal normals.

sections.name: Key Messages
paragraphs: - Scattered showers will return to southeast Utah on Saturday and develop across eastern Utah on Sunday as a Pacific low moves across the Desert Southwest.

- A series of storm systems will move through Utah and southwest Wyoming next week, resulting in periods of cooler weather as temperatures stay near or just below seasonal normals. Confidence is low on the timing and other details of specific systems.

sections.name: Discussion
paragraphs: The piece of a broad Pacific storm system that moved through Utah and southwest Wyoming late night is moving into Canada this evening as the southern branch moves into the Desert Southwest. A few showers linger near the Utah/Idaho border in association with the first piece, but these are rapidly diminishing as the shortwave continues north. Temperatures have been on the cool side today, with maxes running 5-10F below seasonal normals.

The southern branch of the low is on track to slowly move across Arizona on Saturday before turning to the northwest and moving into Colorado on Saturday. This will keep moisture and instability over southern Utah, southeast Utah in particularly, resulting in the development of scattered showers and thunderstorms throughout the day. Overall coverage and duration will be much less than what we saw the past few days, but can't rule out some areas of flash flooding. Once the system starts tracking northeast, the threat of showers will spread across eastern Utah, with the showers primarily focused over the higher terrain east of I-15.

Weak ridging is then expected to move over Utah during the day on Monday, bringing dry conditions with maxes near seasonal normals. However, the storm track over the Pacific coast will remain open (and remain that way throughout the week) in the absence of a Pacific ridge to block incoming systems. Therefore, confidence is high that next week will be wetter than average as a series of storm systems move onshore and track east. However, there remains a good about of ensemble spread with regard to the timing and track of any particular storm system, and therefore confidence remains low with regard to the details about potential impacts for Utah and southwest Wyoming.

2755.travel_advice: Watch for signs of unstable snow such as recent avalanches, cracking in the snow, and audible collapsing. Avoid traveling on or under similar slopes.

product.author: Jason Konigsberg
bottom_line: Heavy rain on Wednesday and Thursday triggered small wet avalanches in the west-Central and Southern Mountains, but this concern is waning as temperatures drop. The most likely place to trigger an avalanche is at the highest elevations (above about 12,500 feet) in the Southern and west-Central Mountains on west, north, and east-facing slopes where new snow has been accumulating and a layer of mid-October snow persists. The Northern Mountains remain mostly bare.

This weekend, a new storm will deliver 4 to 8 inches of snow to the San Juan and Sangre de Cristo Mountains, creating fresh avalanche concerns on upper-elevation, wind-drifted slopes facing west, north, and east. Early-season travelers, including hunters and hikers, should use caution on steep terrain because even shallow snow on grassy slopes, rock slabs, or old snowfields can slide.

We will provide updates as needed until our daily forecasts resume on November 1, 2026. Please continue submitting your field observations, and check our website for real-time weather station data and model forecasts.

product.author: Kevin Studley
hazard_discussion: Avalanche Forecasting Operations Have Come to a Close for the 2026-26 Season
Have a safe spring in the mountains. Continue to remain vigilant and flexible while traveling in the mountains this spring.
OBSERVATIONS

Observations are still greatly appreciated. Spring-time observations are extremely helpful as forecast operations have come to a close. If you're out in the mountains, submit an observation to let the rest of the public know what's going on out there. Even a simple weather observation can be very useful.
• View recent observations HERE
• Submit an observation HERE
• Recent photos and videos HERE
Snow and Avalanche Information
• Dry Slab avalanche problems such as storm slab and wind slab avalanches are most likely during and immediately following a storm.

• Wet Loose avalanches are expected during warmups and (even brief) clear, sunny weather events, and rain events. Watch for pinwheels and rollerballs as an indicator the snow is becoming damp. If you're sinking into soft, mushy snow, it's time to turn around or find a different aspect.

• Wet Slab avalanches become likely during rain events and with multiple nights above freezing. Wet slabs occur when melt water pools and lubricates crusts or older persistent weak layers. Wet slab avalanches are notoriously difficult to predict.
• Cornices are large and often become unstable during prolonged warmups. Give yourself plenty of space above and below them. They tend to begin shedding during warming and/or rain events.
• Dry Loose Snow avalanches are expected during and immediately after a storm, particularly on shaded, north-facing slopes.

• Glide avalanches typically fail in similar spots year after year after an abundance of meltwater has saturated the ground or lower snowpack. Glide avalanches can occur in steep terrain, on smooth grassy slopes or on large slabs of rock. Look for glide cracks opening up during spring.
WEATHER
• Click HERE to view our Weather Station Map page with updated webcams
• Click HERE to view our Weather Tools page
• Spring weather patterns are often erratic and snow conditions can change quickly during spring weather. Be attentive to these changes and remain flexible with your travel plans.
• Rain on snow events can create dangerous avalanche conditions in a short period of time.
• Spring time means a higher sun angle, with direct solar radiation on the snowpack. Even a brief dose of sunshine can quickly alter the snow surface.

• Overcast skies and snow showers can open up to full sunshine in a matter of minutes. Convective snow showers can be spotty and difficult to forecast. Temperatures can vary depending on elevation and unexpected cloud cover can significantly alter a weather forecast.
OTHER CONSIDERATIONS
• Travel
• As people push into steeper, more consequential terrain, remember to maintain safe travel protocols and not let your guard down just because it's sunny and warm.
• During melt-freeze cycles, pay attention to "slide-for-life" circumstances, particularly during morning travel.
• Be mindful of terrain selection and timing. Identify terrain traps and be prepared to avoid/manage them.
• Spring Mindset

• Springtime is when mountain travelers push for bigger objectives. We have greater confidence in the stability of the snowpack and the high sun angle makes us feel ready to charge. As we start stepping out into bigger terrain in the mountains, be mindful of consequences (ask yourself, "If this slides, what will happen?"). Choose your terrain appropriately and manage new/surface snow problems accordingly. Be aware that dynamic weather can have quick impacts on the snow surface. A common theme I've noticed over the last 15 years playing in steep, snowy mountains is that experienced, seasoned people often get caught in small avalanches in big terrain during the spring. We have a tendency to underestimate "manageable" new snow problems like wind slab and loose snow. Pay attention to changing weather and know that small shifts in spring weather can have dramatic impacts on the upper snowpack.
